enrichment.short_title: Hague Convention return of child to South Africa with domestic violence safeguards
key_facts: The father applied under the Hague Convention for return of his nearly 10-year-old daughter S from England to South Africa, where she had been habitually resident.
The mother removed S from South Africa in January 2004 during a troubled marriage marked by alleged domestic violence, firearm incidents and prior cross-border abduction history.
Wrongful removal under Article 3 was admitted; the mother relied on Article 13(b) grave risk and S's objections to return.
The father agreed to extensive protective measures including separate accommodation, non-molestation orders, funding for litigation and maintenance, and psychiatric assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Hague Convention application for summary return following wrongful removal from South Africa to England.
enrichment.outcome: Order for S's return to South Africa subject to compliance with a detailed schedule of protective preconditions; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Article 13(b) requires clear and compelling evidence of grave risk of harm to the child herself, not merely domestic violence to the mother or her distress; where that high threshold is not met but protective measures can secure welfare on return, the court may order return conditional on those safeguards being in place first.
legal_issues: Whether Article 13(b) grave risk of psychological harm was established
Whether S's objections under Article 13 second paragraph warranted refusal to return
What protective measures were required before ordering return to South Africa
Whether a judge at first instance may make findings on disputed written abuse allegations

enrichment.short_title: Hague abduction: child settled in England after four-year concealment
key_facts: An American father and Irish mother married in California in 1994; their daughter S was born that year and lived in California until December 1998.
After a first Hague abduction to Ireland and consent return in 1999, the mother re-abducted S to England in July 1999 and concealed their identity in Liverpool for over four years.
S was traced in October 2003, briefly placed in foster care, then reunited with the mother subject to tagging and other conditions.
Hague proceedings commenced more than one year after wrongful removal, engaging Article 12(2) settlement and Article 13 defences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Resumed substantive hearing of the father's originating summons for Hague Convention return after an earlier judgment on section 5 interim directions.
enrichment.outcome: Return refused because S was settled in her new environment under Article 12(2); directions given for a future determinative hearing on residence and contact under domestic law.
enrichment.ratio: Where proceedings begin more than a year after wrongful removal and the court is satisfied the child is settled in her new environment, the Hague Convention application fails without residual Convention discretion to order return; deliberate concealment does not stop the one-year period running but is material to settlement.
legal_issues: Whether S was settled in England under Article 12(2) of the Hague Convention
Whether Article 18 preserves Convention jurisdiction to order return after one year
Effect of deliberate concealment on the Article 12 time limit and settlement analysis
Whether Article 13(b) grave risk or child's objections would otherwise have succeeded

enrichment.short_title: English jurisdiction over child after wrongful removal from Scotland
key_facts: Mr and Mrs B married in Abu Dhabi; their daughter R, who has Down Syndrome, was born in 1997 and lived in Scotland until September 2000.

Mrs B removed R to England without the father's agreement; the Willesden County Court made ex parte residence and prohibited steps orders in November 2000 without jurisdiction under section 41 FLA 1986.
Mr B did not challenge the English orders or start Scottish proceedings within the one-year deemed Scottish residence period ending September 2001.
Parallel English Children Act proceedings and belated Scottish divorce proceedings led to a sist in Scotland and a High Court refusal to transfer the case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Sumner J's refusal to discharge English Children Act orders and transfer proceedings to Scotland.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; English courts retained jurisdiction to determine residence and contact, with Scottish matrimonial proceedings stayed.
enrichment.ratio: Section 41 FLA 1986 treats a child wrongfully removed from one UK jurisdiction as habitually resident in the place of origin for one year only; after that period the receiving court gains jurisdiction, and an order made without jurisdiction remains valid until discharged rather than being a nullity.
legal_issues: Whether English courts had jurisdiction to make Children Act orders after September 2001
Whether the November 2000 residence order permanently tainted English proceedings
Effect of subsequent Scottish divorce proceedings on English jurisdiction
Whether the Scottish court's sist amounted to declining jurisdiction in favour of England

enrichment.short_title: Stay of Symbicort patent revocation pending EPO opposition
key_facts: Ivax sought to revoke AstraZeneca's European patents for the asthma drug Symbicort on obviousness grounds while parallel opposition proceedings continued at the EPO.
AstraZeneca applied to stay the English revocation action, citing EPO amendment flexibility, risk of inconsistent decisions and wasted costs exceeding £2 million.
Ivax argued commercial urgency to launch a generic product and public interest in NHS savings, but had delayed opposition and English proceedings.
The judge estimated final EPO resolution around 2008–2009 and found Ivax had not demonstrated pressing commercial prejudice justifying parallel litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to stay English patent revocation proceedings pending final EPO opposition and appeal, with alternative dispute over trial date.
enrichment.outcome: Stay granted pending EPO proceedings; had the stay been refused, trial would have been listed for April 2005 rather than December 2004.
enrichment.ratio: The Patents Court will ordinarily stay English revocation proceedings pending EPO resolution where that can be achieved without injustice, but a stay may be refused where delay would cause real commercial prejudice; here Ivax's own delay and inconsistent pursuit of Irish proceedings undermined its urgency case.
legal_issues: Whether English revocation proceedings should be stayed pending EPO opposition
Whether Ivax would suffer injustice from delay in obtaining a UK decision
Whether AstraZeneca would lose legitimate juridical advantage in EPO amendment procedure
What trial date was appropriate if no stay were ordered

enrichment.short_title: Admissibility and jury directions for forensic lip-reading evidence
key_facts: The appeals concerned whether expert lip-reading from video footage was admissible and how juries should be directed about its reliability.
Luttrell was convicted after a 70-day Reading Crown Court trial of conspiracy to handle stolen goods from a £6–7 million computer equipment theft ring.
Dawson and Hamberger were convicted at Lewes Crown Court in separate drug-export cases where lip-reading of poor-quality video was central.
Multiple co-defendants also renewed sentence appeals following convictions for handling stolen goods.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals and renewed applications against trial judges' rulings admitting lip-reading evidence, with related conviction and sentence appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Lip-reading evidence held potentially admissible with tailored jury warnings; Dawson and Hamberger convictions quashed and retrial ordered; Luttrell conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeals refused.
enrichment.ratio: Forensic lip-reading from video is a recognised skill capable of satisfying ordinary tests of relevance and reliability, but juries should usually receive a special Turnbull-type warning about its limitations; unsafe convictions may follow where testing evidence is not adequately summarised or where judges misdirect on use of the video.
legal_issues: Whether lip-reading from video is admissible expert evidence
What directions a trial judge should give the jury about lip-reading evidence
Whether non-disclosure of other lip-reading tests rendered convictions unsafe
Whether sentences for conspiracy to handle stolen goods were manifestly excessive

enrichment.short_title: Tachograph production offences and validity of successive section 99 notices
key_facts: John Mann International Ltd, a road haulier with about ninety vehicles, failed to produce all tachograph record sheets required by VOSA notices.
After initial production of 3,540 sheets, analysis showed missing records and two further section 99 notices identified outstanding charts for 44 vehicles.
The company was convicted on 44 informations for failure to comply with the third notice requiring production by 2 August 2002.
The company argued offences were committed on failure to comply with the first notice and informations were out of time under section 127.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' convictions for failure to produce tachograph records.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions upheld and respondent's costs summarily assessed at £4,818.50.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to comply with a section 99 Transport Act 1968 production notice is a 'do notice' offence complete when the compliance period expires and is not a continuing offence; separate notices may each give rise to prosecution if earlier failures have not already been prosecuted.
legal_issues: Whether failure to produce tachograph records is a continuing offence
Whether prosecution based on the third notice was within six months under section 127
Whether failure to comply with a later notice can create fresh criminal liability for the same missing records

enrichment.short_title: Rent review hypothetical term commencing on original lease date
key_facts: Chancebutton Ltd sought a declaration on the meaning of a rent review clause in a 25-year office lease of Mulliner House, Turnham Green.
The lease was granted in June 1989 but the term was expressed to run from June 1982, with five-yearly reviews including June 2002.
The clause required review against a letting for a term equal to the term originally granted under the lease.
The tenant contended the hypothetical term ran from 1982 for 25 years less one day; the landlord argued a fresh 25-year term from each review date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declaration on construction of a rent review clause at the final review in 2002.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted for the claimants' construction: the hypothetical term commences on the original term start date with the original duration.
enrichment.ratio: Where a rent review clause requires a letting for a term equal to the term originally granted, the natural and commercially sensible construction is a term commencing on the original commencement date for the original duration, not a new 25-year term from each review date.
legal_issues: Whether the hypothetical letting term starts on the original lease commencement date or the review date
How the presumption of reality applies to rent review valuation formulae
Effect of a backdated commencement date where the lease was granted years later

enrichment.short_title: Committal for refusing public examination in bankruptcy
key_facts: Mr Scriven was adjudged bankrupt in March 2000 and ordered to attend a public examination in bankruptcy in June 2001 but refused to give evidence.
After adjourned examination proceedings in August 2001, he again refused to enter the witness box and was committed to six months' imprisonment for contempt in July 2002.
Implementation of the committal was delayed until March 2004; the committal order was not formally served though a warrant was executed.
Mr Scriven argued the August 2001 hearing was about past contempt not examination, and that non-service and unsigned warrant invalidated committal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal out of time against committal for contempt following refusal to submit to public examination in bankruptcy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; six-month committal upheld as neither procedurally unfair nor excessive.
enrichment.ratio: Non-compliance with County Court Rule 29 requirements to serve a committal order does not automatically invalidate committal where the contemnor knew why he was being imprisoned and cannot show prejudice; a bankrupt has no entitlement to conduct money for attendance at public examination under Insolvency Rule 7.41.
legal_issues: Whether the August 2001 hearing was a resumed public examination or a contempt hearing
Whether failure to serve the committal order rendered imprisonment unlawful
Whether a warrant of committal must be signed by a judge to be valid
Whether six months' imprisonment was excessive for contempt in bankruptcy examination

enrichment.short_title: Freshfields restrained from advising Marks and Spencer takeover bidder
key_facts: Freshfields had previously acted for Marks and Spencer on Project George, the Per Una arrangement with George Davies, charging about £200,000.
Freshfields sought to act for Philip Green's Revival consortium in a potential takeover of Marks and Spencer.
Lawrence Collins J granted an injunction restraining Freshfields from acting, stayed until 3 June 2004, on conflict of interest and confidentiality grounds.
Freshfields offered Chinese walls and undertakings not to advise on the Davies arrangements, but the court found these insufficient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against interim injunction restraining solicitors from acting for a takeover consortium.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; injunction upheld on conflict of interest and breach of confidence grounds with costs against Freshfields.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor may not act for a client against a former client where there is a real conflict of interest, even in a different matter, without consent; in takeover situations a hostile bid cannot be assumed away and confidential information cannot adequately be walled off by late Chinese wall arrangements.
legal_issues: Whether Freshfields had a disqualifying conflict of interest from prior Project George work
Whether Bolkiah confidentiality principles barred acting for the bidder
Whether undertakings and Chinese walls could sufficiently protect Marks and Spencer
Whether a broader approach to confidentiality should apply in takeover cases

enrichment.short_title: Enforcement of SEN consent order after statement ceased to be maintained
key_facts: A, a 16-year-old with significant literacy and numeracy difficulties, had a Statement of Special Educational Needs maintained by Southwark.
Judicial review proceedings in April 2003 were settled by consent on 16 June 2003, recording an agreement for five hours weekly individual teaching support.
The SEND Tribunal ordered Southwark to cease maintaining the statement in February 2004, finding A's needs were best met in further education.
A later sought to compel Southwark to provide the five hours' support under paragraph 1 of the consent order despite the statement ceasing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review application to enforce paragraph 1 of a consent order made during earlier SEN judicial review proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; local authority not bound to provide the agreed support after the statement ceased to be maintained.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 1 of the June 2003 consent order mirrored and enforced the SSEN provision and was not intended as a free-standing obligation independent of continued statement maintenance; once the Tribunal ordered cessation of the statement, the consent order obligations fell away.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 1 of the consent order survived cessation of the SSEN
Construction of the consent order against the statutory SEN framework
Whether section 19(4) Education Act 1996 provided an alternative power to fund the support
